changes.to: “Refers to the word or message of the LORD given to the prophets.” Emphasizes the fulfillment of divine promises.

changes.from: Used here for the temple in Jerusalem, reflecting both physical structure and spiritual enterprise directed by divine command.
changes.to: “Used here for the temple in Jerusalem, reflecting both physical structure and spiritual enterprise directed by divine command.”

changes.from: v20: “no prophecy of scripture comes from one’s own interpretation” — The phrase may refer to the origin of prophecy rather than the reader’s activity. The ambiguity is preserved.
changes.to: v20: “no prophecy of scripture comes from one’s own interpretation” — The phrase may refer to the origin of prophecy rather than to private interpretive activity. The syntax remains ambiguous.

changes.from: v22–23: “Single” (ἁπλοῦς) and “evil” (πονηρός) carry idiomatic weight in Hebrew thought, where the “single” or “good” eye refers to generosity and the “evil” eye to greed. The literal translation is preserved; the idiom is left for the reader to hear.
changes.to: v22–23: “Single” (ἁπλοῦς) and “evil” (πονηρός) carry idiomatic weight. In a Semitic idiom, a “good” or “single” eye can suggest generosity, while an “evil” eye can suggest greed.

changes.from: Hypocrite, literally one who plays a part on a stage. The metaphor is theatrical, not moralistic.
changes.to: “Hypocrite, literally one who plays a part on a stage.” The metaphor is theatrical, not moralistic.

changes.from: “Glory.” Denotes divine presence and radiance; often associated with revelation.

changes.from: “Spirit.” The divine presence given to believers.
